subject: modeling habitat relationships with estimated densities

messages.author: 0c8e4d9395a2aae5
messages.subject: modeling habitat relationships with estimated densities
parts:
Hello Unmarked Users,

I'd like to analyze habitat relationships for birds at the level of twelve, ~50 ha forest stands, each containing around a dozen point counts.  I estimated abundance at the point-count level using temporary emigration (gmultmix) models in Unmarked.  I followed Royle 2004 to expand these estimates to the level of entire stands, summing the estimated abundances of each point count and dividing by the total area sampled.  I used parametric bootstrapping to get a confidence interval for each stand-level density estimate.  Below I show some of the bootstrap data for Eastern Wood-pewee (200 simulations, with 0 indicating the original density estimate) and a graph of the 95% confidence intervals. 

Now I'm not sure how to proceed.  I could run a set of models with stand-level covariates and evaluate with AIC.  But how do I incorporate the uncertainty of the stand-level density estimates?  Do I need to incorporate it?  It seems like I should given the width of the confidence intervals.  I'd really appreciate any thoughts on this. 


Mike Worland

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: modeling habitat relationships with estimated densities
parts: Hi Mike, I think you could do some kind of weighted regression on your bootstrap output as a second stage analysis, otherwise you'd need to use a fully explicit hierarchical model in BUGS to estimate stand-level relationships.  The latter approach is technically better for incorporating the uncertainty, but the former approach could provide a good approximation and allow you to still use AIC.  Either way, with only 12 stands you'd have to keep the stand-level models fairly simple (i.e., univariate relationships)

Thanks a lot for your reply, Dan.  Here's some of the script I just tried, attempting to follow the first approach you advised, and some output. 
 
I weighted with the SE calculated from the bootstrapping--I just took the standard deviation of the bootstrapped values for each stand.  Is that correct? 
 
And then I used the below linear mixed models where I treated block as a random effect.  I have 3 blocks, each with 4 stands.  As you say, I've got sample size issues here, but the results have been reasonable so far.  Do you see red flags with this analysis?

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: modeling habitat relationships with estimated densities
parts:
Hi Mike, I believe the weights should be the reciprocal of the variance: 1/(se^2).

Admittedly, I typically take my second recommended approach in BUGS simply because I'm familiar with it.  A good paper on the subject of weighted vs. unweighted regression is Fletcher & Dixon (2012) MEE, where they show that weighted regression is not necessarily better than unweighted.  Essentially, if you're going to take a simpler route with a 2-stage analysis instead of separating the measurement and process errors explicitly with a hierarchical model, the approximation from an unweighted regression is probably adequate.

Also, with only 3 blocks and 4 stands per block, your block random effect might be overkill (or more reason to go Bayesian).  Either way, maybe others can chime in here with some thoughts.
